source_title: Unlawful Use of an Unmanned Aircraft System Related to Infrastructure — Unlawful Use of an Unmanned Aircraft System Related to Images
citation: Ark. Code Ann. § 5-60-103 (Act 2015-1019, as substantially amended and retitled by Act 2025-597 (the "Arkansas Privacy Act"), eff. 2025-08-05; previously amended by Acts 2019-320, 2019-508, 2019-1000, 2021-140)
uas_topic: Critical infrastructure UAS restriction; UAS image-capture/surveillance restriction
regulated_activity: (1) Using a UAS to conduct surveillance of, gather evidence or collect information about, or photographically/electronically record 'critical infrastructure' (now expressly including natural gas distribution/transmission lines, facilities, and storage, added by Act 2025-597) without the owner's prior written consent; and (2), as a newly created separate offense effective 2025-08-05, purposely using a UAS to capture an 'image' (defined broadly to include sound, thermal, infrared, ultraviolet, visible-light, or other electromagnetic-wave or odor data) of an individual or private property with the purpose of conducting surveillance on that individual or property
requirement_type: Prohibition (misdemeanor), with property-owner, retained-contractor, insurance, law-enforcement, and ArDOT/State Highway Commission/public-works exceptions (critical-infrastructure offense, subsection (c)); separate prohibition (misdemeanor) on purposeful surveillance-intent image capture of a person or private property, with an image-destruction defense, a § 27-118-101 lawful-capture defense, and a law-enforcement-duties defense (new 'images' offense, subsections (e)-(f))
summary: Ark. Code Ann. § 5-60-103 was substantially amended and retitled by Act 2025-597 (the Arkansas Privacy Act, HB1148, approved 2025-04-14, effective 2025-08-05 with no emergency clause). The pre-existing critical-infrastructure offense (subsections (a)-(d)) is preserved with two changes: the definition of 'critical infrastructure' now expressly includes 'a natural gas distribution or transmission line, natural gas facility, or natural gas storage' (new subdivision (a)(1)(I)), and a new consent-exception subdivision (c)(4) was added exempting the Arkansas Department of Transportation, the State Highway Commission, a city or county department of public works, and their contractors/consultants/employees/partner state entities performing authorized department/commission/public-works work. It remains a Class B misdemeanor (Class A for a second or subsequent offense) to knowingly use a UAS to conduct surveillance of, gather evidence about, or record critical infrastructure without the owner's prior written consent, subject to the pre-existing property-owner/retained-contractor and insurance-underwriting exceptions. The Act also adds an entirely new offense at subsections (e)-(f): a person commits 'unlawful use of an unmanned aircraft system related to images' — a Class C misdemeanor — if the person purposely uses a UAS to capture an image of an individual or private property with the purpose of conducting surveillance on that individual or property. It is a defense that the person destroyed the image as soon as they knew it was captured in violation of the section (without having disclosed it), that the image was captured lawfully as authorized under the Act's new safe-harbor statute § 27-118-101 (AR-011), or that the image was captured by a law enforcement officer performing official duties. NOTE ON A DRAFTING ANOMALY: the enrolled Act 597 text's UAS-definition exclusion at subdivision (a)(3)(B)(iv) reads, verbatim, 'An unmanned aircraft system used under a certificate of authorization issued by the operated by a person for a commercial purpose pursuant to and in compliance with Federal Aviation Administration regulations, authorizations, or exemptions' — this appears to be an uncorrected drafting/amendment-stacking artifact (the clause reads as though two successive amendments were merged without cleanup) rather than a deliberate substantive change; it should be rechecked against the eventual official codified/Justia text once available, since the current wording is grammatically broken and its exact legal effect on the COA exclusion is not free from doubt.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Screen the project map for protected critical-infrastructure facilities (now including natural gas lines/facilities/storage) and active emergency operations before dispatch. Separately, because the new 'images' offense turns on purposeful surveillance intent rather than subject matter, ensure flight planning, camera framing, and mission purpose documentation for any AEC survey/inspection work make clear the flight's purpose is mapping, engineering, or infrastructure documentation — not surveillance of a specific individual or private property — and rely on the new § 27-118-101 safe harbor (AR-011), which expressly covers Arkansas-licensed engineers and surveyors performing mapping/land-surveying/GIS work, as a documented lawful-use basis.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Treat the cited authority as a documented compliance gate where applicable, now spanning two distinct offenses (critical-infrastructure surveillance and general surveillance-intent image capture) plus a new civil-liability exposure under AR-009 and a new possession/disclosure offense under AR-010. Preserve the facts supporting any exception, consent, or § 27-118-101 safe-harbor theory, allocate client and operator responsibilities clearly, and seek state counsel when project facts approach ambiguous or penal language — including the noted drafting anomaly in the COA exclusion clause.
verification_status: Full current statutory text (as amended through Act 2025-597, approved 2025-04-14, effective 2025-08-05) verified directly against the official enrolled Act 597 PDF at arkleg.state.ar.us. Not yet cross-checked against Justia's codification, which had not yet incorporated the 2025 regular session's amendments as of this research pass; recommend re-confirming against Justia or the official Arkansas Code once its 2025-session update is published.
notes: Act 2025-597 was a significant, previously unrecorded legislative event for this register: it retitled and expanded § 5-60-103, added a wholly new UAS-images criminal offense (subsections (e)-(f)), and (via the same Act) created three additional new authorities now recorded separately as AR-009 (new civil action, § 16-118-119), AR-010 (new possession/disclosure offense, § 5-60-126), and AR-011 (new statewide lawful-use safe harbor naming AR-licensed engineers/surveyors, § 27-118-101) — AR-011 in particular is the single most AEC-relevant new Arkansas authority identified in this retrofit pass. The COA exclusion drafting anomaly noted in the summary field does not appear to change the ordinary-commercial-Part-107-operator analysis carried over from the pre-2025 text: a routine commercial AEC drone flight over critical infrastructure without the owner's consent is still not automatically exempted merely because the operator holds a Part 107 remote pilot certificate.

summary: Ark. Code Ann. § 5-16-101(b) makes it unlawful to knowingly use an unmanned vehicle or aircraft, camcorder, motion picture camera, photographic camera, or other equipment that is concealed, operated to escape detection, or disguised, to secretly or surreptitiously videotape, film, photograph, record, or electronically view another person's body where that person has a reasonable expectation of privacy, without the person's knowledge or consent. A violation is a Class B misdemeanor, elevated to a Class A misdemeanor if the recording is distributed, posted online, or the person has a prior conviction under this section or § 5-16-102 (AR-004). Subsection (d) exempts several categories of authorized monitoring (court-ordered, security monitoring by an occupant/owner/administrator, correctional-facility security monitoring, and law-enforcement monitoring within official duties), none of which are general commercial-UAS-operator exceptions.

source_title: Civil Action for Damages Caused by Violation of the Unmanned Aircraft System Image-Capture and Possession/Disclosure Offenses
regulated_party: Any person who violates § 5-60-103 (images offense, AR-001) or § 5-60-126 (AR-010)
regulated_activity: Capturing, or possessing/disclosing/displaying/distributing/otherwise using, an image in violation of §§ 5-60-103 or 5-60-126
requirement_type: Civil liability: an owner or tenant of private real property whose property or person (while on the property, with a reasonable expectation of privacy) was imaged in violation of § 5-60-103 may enjoin the violation, recover $5,000 in statutory civil damages per episode of unlawful image capture, $10,000 per episode of unlawful disclosure/display/distribution/other use in violation of § 5-60-126, or actual damages if the image was disclosed/displayed/distributed with malice; plus mandatory court costs and reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party. Two-year statute of limitations.
summary: Ark. Code Ann. § 16-118-119, added by Act 2025-597 (the Arkansas Privacy Act) as a new section within Title 16, Chapter 118, Subchapter 1, gives an owner or tenant of private real property a private civil action against a person who, in violation of § 5-60-103 (AR-001), captured an image of the property or of the owner/tenant while on the property with a reasonable expectation of privacy. Remedies include injunctive relief, statutory damages of $5,000 per episode of unlawful capture (or $10,000 per episode of unlawful disclosure/display/distribution/other use of an image in violation of the companion possession/disclosure offense at § 5-60-126, AR-010), or actual damages where disclosure/display/distribution was done with 'malice' (a defined term: specific intent to cause substantial injury or harm to the property owner/tenant). All owners of a parcel are treated as a single owner and all tenants as a single tenant for damages purposes. The court must award costs and reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party. An action must be commenced within two years of the capture or the initial unlawful disclosure/display/distribution/use.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This is a companion civil-liability statute to the new images offense (AR-001, subsections (e)-(f)) and the new possession/disclosure offense (AR-010); it exposes an AEC operator to a statutory-minimum-damages claim, mandatory attorney's-fee shifting, and injunctive relief independent of any criminal misdemeanor charge, and is distinct from AR-002's pre-existing critical-infrastructure-only civil action under § 16-118-111.

summary: Ark. Code Ann. § 5-60-126, added by Act 2025-597 as a new section within Title 5, Chapter 60, Subchapter 1, makes it a separate offense to possess, disclose, display, distribute, or otherwise use an image that was captured in violation of the new § 5-60-103 images offense (AR-001). A violation is a Class C misdemeanor if the person only possessed the image, or a Class B misdemeanor if the person otherwise disclosed, displayed, distributed, or used it; each image is a separate offense, and it is a defense that the person destroyed the image (for a possession charge) or stopped disclosing/displaying/distributing/using it (for a disclosure-type charge) as soon as they knew it was captured unlawfully, or that the image was lawfully captured under the new § 27-118-101 safe harbor (AR-011).

source_title: Use of Unmanned Aircraft System to Capture Image — Statewide Lawful-Use Safe Harbor (25 Enumerated Categories, Including Licensed Engineers and Surveyors)
citation: Ark. Code Ann. § 27-118-101 (Act 2025-597, § 5, creating Ark. Code Title 27, Subtitle 8, Chapter 118, eff. 2025-08-05)
uas_topic: UAS image-capture safe harbor / permitted uses
regulated_party: Any person capturing a UAS image in Arkansas; expressly includes Arkansas-licensed engineers and surveyors, utilities, ArDOT/public-works-affiliated persons, insurers, real-estate brokers, higher-education and Game & Fish Commission researchers, assessors, critical-infrastructure operators, and law enforcement
regulated_activity: Capturing an image using a UAS in Arkansas
requirement_type: Statutory safe harbor: capturing an image under any of 25 enumerated circumstances is expressly declared lawful and operates as a defense to the § 5-60-103 images offense (AR-001) and the § 5-60-126 possession/disclosure offense (AR-010); it is not itself a permit or approval process.
summary: Ark. Code Ann. § 27-118-101, added by Act 2025-597 as a new Chapter 118 ('Unmanned Aircraft Systems') within Title 27, Subtitle 8, declares it lawful to capture a UAS image in Arkansas under any of 25 enumerated circumstances, several of direct AEC relevance: (23) by an engineer or surveyor licensed in the State of Arkansas for the purpose of mapping and land-surveying tasks or collecting geographic information system (GIS) data supporting public or private infrastructure — an express, named statutory safe harbor for core AEC drone survey/mapping work; (24) operation by or on behalf of a critical-infrastructure owner/operator for siting, deploying, inspecting, monitoring, operating, or maintaining the facility; (5) utility (electric, natural gas, water/wastewater) inspection, maintenance, vegetation-clearance, and routing/siting work; (21) work by an employee, consultant, or contractor acting on behalf of the Arkansas Department of Transportation, State Highway Commission, Arkansas Highway Police Division, or a city/county department of public works; (6) capture with the consent of the individual who owns or lawfully occupies the property; (14) capture from no more than eight feet above ground level in a public place without magnification; and (15) capture of public real property (or property of a state-supported institution of higher education) or a person on such property. Other categories cover higher-education/Game & Fish research, FAA-designated UAS test ranges, U.S. military operations, satellite-captured mapping images, search-warrant-authorized law enforcement use, various emergency/public-safety/search-and-rescue law-enforcement categories, real-estate marketing by a licensed broker (no identifiable individuals), pipeline inspection/safety, port-authority security, and property-assessor use with owner consent. Subsection (c) clarifies the section does not apply to the manufacture, assembly, distribution, or sale of an unmanned aircraft (i.e., it is not an equipment-commerce provision). Subdivision (b)(20) references 'a surveyor within the Department of Transformation and Shared Services' — a real Arkansas state agency created by a 2023 government reorganization — for mapping and land-surveying tasks; this appears deliberate rather than a drafting error but was not independently cross-verified against that department's current organization in this pass.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This is the single most directly relevant new Arkansas authority for AEC UAS work: subdivision (b)(23) names Arkansas-licensed engineers and surveyors performing mapping, land-surveying, or infrastructure-supporting GIS data collection as an express statutory safe harbor. Confirm and document the licensee's current Arkansas PE/PS licensure, frame mission purpose and deliverables as mapping/surveying/GIS work, and keep that documentation on file alongside any project-specific consent or critical-infrastructure-operator authorization, since the safe harbor is a defense that depends on the facts of the capture matching an enumerated category.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: For public-agency or ArDOT-affiliated work, confirm the specific enumerated category relied upon (e.g., subdivision (21) for ArDOT/public-works-affiliated persons, or (15) for public real property) and retain the authorizing engagement or contract documentation.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified; subsection (c) expressly excludes UAS manufacture, assembly, distribution, or sale from this section.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Treat this as an affirmative defense/safe-harbor structure rather than a permit system — the burden in practice will fall on demonstrating the capture fit an enumerated category. Build project files that map each AEC engagement to a specific subdivision (most often (23) or (24)) and preserve licensure and engagement records accordingly.
